strengths: The paper addresses a practical image-stitching problem: residual misalignment that seam selection alone cannot conceal. Repairing problematic regions through local dense alignment and constrained seam recomputation is a useful, modular approach.

Figures 1, 7, 10, and 11 show credible improvements to structures such as curbs and stairs. These examples support the central motivation that modifying local alignment can resolve artifacts that persist when only the seam changes.

Evaluation covers 79 image pairs across three datasets, including two public datasets, and reports runtime comparisons. The user study provides additional perceptual evidence: the proposed method receives 108 of 160 first-place votes on the selected examples.

The manuscript attributes its main borrowed methods and public datasets, reports several important parameter settings, and provides helpful pipeline illustrations. Section 4.4 and Figure 12 candidly explain failures under widespread misalignment or large residual displacement.
weaknesses: The technical advance is incremental, combining the seam-quality evaluation of [17], SIFT flow [20], sigmoid flow modification, and constrained graph-cut recomposition. Figure 4 provides a useful qualitative smoothing example, but there are no dataset-level ablations establishing the benefits of the proposed modification over ordinary local SIFT flow or simpler spatial weighting. The contribution of seam recomputation is also not isolated.

The central warp is underspecified. Section 3.4 describes applying f(V(p)) to a displacement vector, whereas Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid whose argument is subsequently described as a normalized spatial coordinate. The actual vector transformation, its orientation for general seams, and its treatment of patch boundaries are unclear. Patch padding, overlapping repair regions, and SIFT-flow settings also need clarification for faithful reproduction.

The quantitative comparisons include only seam-cutting methods [16] and [17] with a fixed initial aligner. Competing methods that also modify alignment, particularly [18] and [26], receive only a selected qualitative comparison. Relevant cited approaches such as residual warping [12] and edge-guided composition [5] are not evaluated. Consequently, the experiments establish improvement over the chosen seam-cutting baselines more convincingly than the broader state-of-the-art claims.

The principal quantitative measure, Equation (5), uses the same SSIM signal that guides repair and evaluates only the seam neighborhood; it does not establish preservation of geometry throughout the repaired patches. The paper itself identifies a disagreement between this metric and perceived quality. The user study helps, but its eight manually selected 'controversial' examples, unspecified presentation randomization, and lack of per-image results or uncertainty estimates limit generalization.

The claim that the method can almost remove the rough-alignment assumption exceeds the demonstrated scope. Section 3.4 assumes small residual parallax within extracted patches, and Section 4.4 acknowledges dependence on an initially mostly correct seam. Moreover, the max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) acceptance rule in Section 3.3 can accept uniformly high-error seams. Controlled evaluation across residual-displacement levels and alternative initial aligners is needed to establish the operating range and claimed generality.
